paragraphs:
R. Nehorai, Avot 4; Mishnah Nazir 9:5; Kiddushin 4:14. This is R. Neḥemyah (see his entry). Shabbat 147b and Eruvin 13b: his name was not Meir but Nehorai—the true reading is 'Meyasha,' contrary to Maimonides' claim that Meir is Nehorai. Why was he called Meir? He illuminated the sages' eyes in halakhah. His name was not Nehorai but Neḥemyah; some say Elazar ben Arakh. Why Nehorai? He illuminated the sages' eyes in halakhah. Yuḥasin writes [in Seder HaDorot]: Eruvin's statement adds a second sage with two names because Meir also bore the name Meyasha. As Meyasha was called Meir, a term for light, so Neḥemyah was called Nehorai, a term for light; this is Elazar ben Arakh. (I likewise saw T.Ḥ. [ת״ח; provisionally Torat Ḥayyim] in Eruvin explain it. Melo Ratzon 96c attributes this explanation to the eminent R. Shemuel, R. Ḥayyim Yeshayah [name string requires review], and praises it, without seeing Yuḥasin and Torat Ḥayyim had already said it.) Arvei Pesaḥim similarly, after mentioning one sage with many names, mentions others: Issi ben Gamliel, Yosef of Hutzal, R. Yitzḥak Nappaḥa (see his entry). Later I found that Rabbenu Ḥananel explained that Meir was called Meyasha, Neḥemyah was Nehorai, and Elazar ben Arakh too was called Nehorai.

That Nehorai was Neḥemyah seems also Rashi's view, Sanhedrin 20b: 'Neḥemyah says, etc.; Nehorai says'—not our current reading, but Yalkut, Shemuel I§8. Rashi explains that this is absent from Tosefta and erroneous in the books, since Eruvin establishes Neḥemyah as Nehorai. But saying Nehorai was Elazar ben Arakh is incorrect: Mishnah, end of Nazir 66, has Nehorai disagree with Yose; end of Kiddushin has him disagree with Meir and Yehudah. Rosh HaShanah 22b tells of Nehorai going to a witness to testify about him on Shabbat at Usha before Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi's father. Elazar ben Arakh did not live in their time; see his entry. (Our Gemara does not expressly state Nehorai came before Shimon ben Gamliel, but he came to Usha, where the Sanhedrin sat in Shimon ben Gamliel's time; see Rabban Gamliel the elder.) Maimonides' Meir=Nehorai assertion is also incorrect: first chapter of Sanhedrin says Akiva ordained Meir and they did not accept him; Yehudah ben Bava ordained Meir, Yose, Elazar ben Shammua, Yehudah and Shimon; Rav Avya adds Neḥemyah. Thus Meir and Neḥemyah are separate. Anonymous Mishnah is Meir; anonymous Tosefta is Neḥemyah (see Akiva). End of Yuḥasin.

Meir and Neḥemyah disagree in Sotah 12, 13; Megillah 15b. Ḥelek 99a: Meir says, Natan says, Neḥemyah says; Sifra: Nehorai says, etc. Berakhot 40a: Meir says, Neḥemyah says, Yehudah says; Nedarim 31b: Neḥemyah says, Meir says. But why Rashi and Yuḥasin decided Nehorai was Neḥemyah from the Gemara's apparent wording requires examination. Midrash Rabbah, Ekev, has Nehorai and Neḥemyah disagree: 'What did they see,' etc. Midrash Ruth has Nehorai say that Neḥemyah said the Shema contains 248 words; it objects that there are 245, and answers that the prayer leader repeats 'The Lord your God is true.' Ḥelek 97a separately teaches: Nehorai says the generation when David's son comes will have youths shame, etc.; Neḥemyah says insolence will increase. Ruth Rabbah, 'I went away full': Elijah of blessed memory asked Nehorai about 'Shaḥarayim begot in Moab's field,' I Chronicles 8 (see below, Nehorai [נהוריי]). Elijah asked him. In R. Yehoshua's name, Temurah 14b; Bamidbar Rabbah 10. R. Yehudah son of R. Simon in his name. R. Pelippas spoke to him. Nehorai's burial is at Akhbara (see R. Yannai).
